To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the variability inherent to the sequencing of 16 S rRNA amplicon libraries is significant enough to swamp the underlying variation in bacterial community composition over diurnal time-scale in drinking water.

(1) the extent and pattern (presence/absence and relative abundance of taxa) of diurnal changes in drinking water microbial community is specific to each location, (2) the extent of diurnal changes can vary across time-periods within the same day, and (3) diurnal changes in microbial community are likely driven by hydraulic changes in drinking water systems.

the extent and magnitude of diurnal changes in drinking water bacteria community composition varies by location and is driven by changes in both the presence/absense of low abundance bacteria and shifts in relative abundance of dominant taxa, and the extent of variability inherent to the sequencing and PCR amplification steps is large enough to mask differences in bacterial communities from replicate sampling sites.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the impact of sampling, amplification, and sequencing on the characterization of bacterial community changes over diurnal time scales in drinking water systems and provides a foundation for understanding the dynamics of drinking water bacterial communities in general.
the effect of sampling, PCR and sequencing replication on the ability to detect changes in bacterial communities over diurnal time scales.
the impact of PCR/sequencing variability on discerning diurnal dynamics of drinking water bacterial community.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sampling and method biases associated with amplicon sequencing can be overcome by replication at multiple levels.
the variability in the detection of low abundance taxa across PCR and sequencing replicates is significant enough to obscure the underlying temporal dynamics of bacterial community.
the sampling, PCR, sequencing, and bioinformatics steps are all important in determining bacterial community composition, and the extent of variability inherent to these steps can be substantial.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
whilst the PCR and sequencing steps introduce significant intra-sample variability, they can be used to capture subtle diurnal changes in drinking water systems.

the variability inherent to the sampling, PCR and sequencing steps can mask underlying systematic differences in the bacterial community, particularly when the differences are subtle or the community is dominated by a few taxa.
the variability in PCR amplification and high throughput sequencing is large enough to swamp any subtle changes in bacterial community composition that may arise from hydraulic changes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
whilst high throughput sequencing is a powerful tool, it must be used in a manner that is cognizant of the variability associated with each step of the process.

high-throughput sequencing of bacterial communities in bulk water can provide meaningful insights into the dynamics of drinking water bacterial communities, but that the extent and nature of these dynamics are likely to be highly dependent on the sampling site.
the variability inherent to PCR amplification and high-throughput sequencing of 16s rRNA gene amplicons is significant enough to potentially mask differences between samples.
